An **ore** of magnesium must be a mineral from which magnesium can be extracted — so it must
**contain magnesium**.
**(1) Carnallite**, KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O ✓ a magnesium ore, and the usual source for extracting the
metal by electrolysis of the fused chloride
**(2) Dolomite**, MgCO₃·CaCO₃ ✓ a mixed carbonate of magnesium and calcium
**(4) Sea water** ✓ an important commercial source: it contains about 0·13 % magnesium as
MgCl₂, precipitated as Mg(OH)₂ with lime and then converted to the chloride
**(3) Calamine** ✗ **not a magnesium ore** — this is the answer. Calamine is **zinc
carbonate, ZnCO₃**, an ore of **zinc**, not magnesium.
The name is the whole difficulty here, since nothing in it suggests which metal it holds.
The zinc ores are worth collecting together, because they are commonly confused with one
another:
**Calamine** ZnCO₃
**Zinc blende** (sphalerite) ZnS — the chief ore
**Zincite** ZnO
Calamine is also familiar outside the laboratory as the pink **calamine lotion** used on
skin, which is zinc oxide with a trace of iron oxide.
∴ calamine.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|2||0|0:
The configuration given is **1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰**. Add up the electrons:
2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 10 = **28 electrons**
So the species has 28 electrons. Now find which option that fits.
**(1) Cu⁺** ✓ — copper has Z = 29, so Cu⁺ has 29 − 1 = **28 electrons**. And its
configuration really is [Ar] **3d¹⁰**, since copper loses its single 4s electron first ✓
**(4) Ni** ✗ — nickel also has **28 electrons**, so the count alone does not rule it out. But
the **arrangement** is wrong: neutral nickel is [Ar] **3d⁸ 4s²**, not 3d¹⁰. The 4s orbital
fills before 3d, so a neutral atom of Z = 28 keeps two electrons in 4s. This is the real
trap in the question.
**(2) Cu²⁺** ✗ — 29 − 2 = **27 electrons**, giving [Ar]3d⁹.
**(3) Ni²⁺** ✗ — 28 − 2 = **26 electrons**, giving [Ar]3d⁶.
So both Cu⁺ and Ni have 28 electrons, and only the **distribution** distinguishes them.
The reason Cu⁺ ends up as 3d¹⁰ is the stability of the **completely filled d subshell**: it
is also why neutral copper is 3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than 3d⁹4s², and why Cu⁺ is colourless and
diamagnetic while Cu²⁺ is blue and paramagnetic.
∴ Cu⁺.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|3||0|0:
Identify the four elements from their configurations — all are period-3 elements built on a
neon core:
(1) [Ne] 3s² 3p¹ = **aluminium**, IE₁ = 577 kJ mol⁻¹
(3) [Ne] 3s² 3p² = **silicon**, IE₁ = 786
(2) [Ne] 3s² 3p³ = **phosphorus**, IE₁ = **1012** ✓ highest
(4) [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ = **sulphur**, IE₁ = 1000
The general trend — ionisation energy rising from left to right across a period — takes us as
far as Al < Si < P, but it would then put sulphur higher still. It does not: **phosphorus
beats sulphur**, and that reversal is what the question is testing.
**Why phosphorus is anomalously high.** Its 3p subshell is **exactly half filled**, 3p³, with
one electron in each of the three p orbitals and all spins parallel. That arrangement is
spherically symmetrical and carries the maximum **exchange energy**, so it is unusually
stable and an electron is hard to remove.
**Why sulphur is lower.** Its 3p⁴ configuration forces **two electrons to share one orbital**.
Their mutual repulsion in that small region makes one of them comparatively easy to remove —
and removing it leaves the stable half-filled p³ behind, which is a further incentive.
The same reversal appears at **N > O** in period 2, for exactly the same reason.
∴ [Ne] 3s² 3p³.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|4||0|0:
Work out the oxidation number of bromine on each side.
**In Br₂** — an **element in its free state**, so by definition every atom has oxidation
number **zero**.
**In BrO₃⁻** — let the oxidation number of Br be x. Oxygen is **−2** in an oxoanion, and the
sum must equal the charge on the ion, **−1**:
x + 3(−2) = −1
x − 6 = −1
**x = +5**
So bromine goes from **zero to +5** ✓ — option (1).
The change is an **oxidation**: each bromine atom loses five electrons. (In the
disproportionation of bromine in alkali, Br₂ + 2OH⁻ ⟶ Br⁻ + BrO⁻ + H₂O and further, some
bromine is oxidised to bromate while the rest is reduced to bromide — so the same element
goes both up and down.)
The two things to be careful about are both in the distractors. **Option (2)** assumes
bromine starts at +1, but an element in its elemental form is always **zero**, whatever its
electronegativity. **Option (3)**, zero to −3, has the sign wrong: −3 would mean bromine had
**gained** electrons, which is what happens when it becomes Br⁻, and even then the value is
−1, not −3.
A useful check: bromate is a strong oxidising agent precisely because bromine in it is in a
**high** positive state and readily falls back.
∴ zero to +5.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|7||0|0:
The strength of a hydrogen bond X–H·····Y depends on two things: how **electronegative** the
atoms X and Y are, and how **small** they are. The more electronegative X is, the more
positive the hydrogen becomes; the smaller Y is, the more concentrated its lone pair and the
closer it can approach.
Only **N, O and F** are electronegative and small enough to form proper hydrogen bonds, and
**fluorine is the most electronegative element there is** (4·0).
**(3) F–H·····F** ✓ **strongest.** Both partners are fluorine, so the H–F bond is maximally
polarised and the acceptor lone pair is maximally concentrated. This is the strongest
hydrogen bond known, about **40 kJ mol⁻¹** — nearly ten times a typical van der Waals
interaction, and strong enough to make HF₂⁻ a real species.
The others are weaker:
**(4) O–H·····N** and the O–H·····O bonds of water come next, at roughly 20–25 kJ mol⁻¹
**(2) O–H·····S** ✗ sulphur is large and only moderately electronegative (2·5), so its lone
pair is diffuse and the bond is very weak
**(1) S–H·····O** ✗ weaker still: sulphur as the donor barely polarises the H at all
The strength of the H–F bond is why **HF boils at 19·5 °C** while HCl boils at −85 °C, and
why HF is the only hydrohalic acid that is weak in water.
∴ F–H·····F.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|8||0|0:
**Step 1 — moles of CO₂.** At STP one mole of any gas occupies 22·4 dm³:
n(CO₂) = 11·2 / 22·4 = **0·5 mol**
**Step 2 — write the neutralisation.** Carbon dioxide is a **dibasic** acid anhydride: with
excess alkali it gives the **carbonate**, so **two** moles of KOH are needed for each mole of
CO₂:
CO₂ + **2**KOH ⟶ K₂CO₃ + H₂O
**Step 3 — moles of KOH.**
n(KOH) = 2 × 0·5 = **1·0 mol**
**Step 4 — convert to grams.** The molar mass of KOH is 39 + 16 + 1 = **56 g mol⁻¹**:
mass = 1·0 × 56 = **56 g** ✓
The **factor of 2** is what the question is really testing. Taking a 1 : 1 ratio — as if the
product were the **bi**carbonate, KHCO₃ — gives 0·5 mol and 28 g, which is option (2) and sits
there waiting for exactly that mistake. The word **'completely'** in the question is what
fixes the product as the normal carbonate.
The mass of CaCO₃ decomposed is not asked for, but it follows: 0·5 mol of CO₂ needs 0·5 mol
of CaCO₃, which is 50 g.
∴ 56 g.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|11||0|0:
Set out the amounts before and after reaction.
**The reaction:**
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃
**Step 1 — how much O₂ reacts.** 25 % of the 4 moles present:
O₂ used = 0·25 × 4 = **1 mol**
**Step 2 — use the stoichiometry.** One mole of O₂ consumes **two** moles of SO₂ and produces
**two** moles of SO₃:
SO₂ used = **2 mol**
SO₃ formed = **2 mol**
**Step 3 — amounts at equilibrium.**
SO₂ : 4 − 2 = **2 mol**
O₂ : 4 − 1 = **3 mol**
SO₃ : 0 + 2 = **2 mol**
**Step 4 — total.**
2 + 3 + 2 = **7·0 mol** ✓
A quick check on the arithmetic: the reaction converts **3** moles of gas into **2**, so the
total must **fall** from the original 8 moles by exactly the extent of reaction, 1 mole:
8 − 1 = 7 ✓
That check is worth doing, because the commonest error is to take 25 % of the **SO₂** rather
than the O₂ — which would give O₂ used = 0·5, a total of 7·5, and no option to match.
The question says '25 % of O₂ is used up', and the stoichiometric ratios must then be applied
in the right direction.
∴ 7·0.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|16||0|0:
In an **Ellingham diagram** the standard free energy of oxide formation, ΔG°, is plotted
against temperature. Since
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
the **slope of each line is −ΔS°**. So a line slopes **downwards** only when ΔS° is
**positive** — that is, when the reaction **increases** the number of moles of gas.
Count the gas moles in each (solids contribute nothing):
**(1) Mg + ½O₂ ⟶ MgO** — gas: ½ ⟶ 0. Δn = **−½**, ΔS° negative, line slopes **up** ✗
**(2) 2Ag + ½O₂ ⟶ Ag₂O** — gas: ½ ⟶ 0. Δn = **−½**, slopes up ✗
**(4) CO + ½O₂ ⟶ CO₂** — gas: 1½ ⟶ 1. Δn = **−½**, slopes up ✗
**(3) C + ½O₂ ⟶ CO** — gas: ½ ⟶ **1**. Δn = **+½**, ΔS° **positive**, so the line slopes
**downwards** ✓
This single downward line is the most important feature of the whole diagram, and it is why
**carbon is the universal reducing agent in metallurgy**. As the temperature rises, the C/CO
line falls while every metal-oxide line rises, so sooner or later the carbon line passes
**below** the metal's line — and above that temperature carbon can reduce the oxide.
That crossing point is what fixes the operating temperature of a blast furnace.
∴ C + ½O₂ ⟶ CO.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|17||0|0:
An **endothermic** reaction absorbs heat; an **exothermic** one gives it out. Take the four
reactions of the blast furnace in turn.
**(1) CaCO₃ ⟶ CaO + CO₂** ✓ **endothermic.** This is the **thermal decomposition** of the
limestone charged into the furnace. Bonds are only broken, nothing is burnt, and the
reaction needs about **+178 kJ mol⁻¹**. It happens in the middle zone of the furnace at
about 1100 K, and the lime produced then slags off the silica impurities.
The others all **release** heat:
**(2) 2C + O₂ ⟶ 2CO** ✗ the **combustion** of coke in the hot air blast, ΔH ≈ −221 kJ. This
is the furnace's main source of heat.
**(3) C + O₂ ⟶ CO₂** ✗ complete combustion, ΔH ≈ −393 kJ, more exothermic still.
**(4) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO ⟶ 2Fe + 3CO₂** ✗ the actual **reduction** of the ore, mildly exothermic,
ΔH ≈ −25 kJ.
So three of the four supply heat and one consumes it.
The general signal is worth carrying away: **decompositions are usually endothermic** —
bonds are broken and nothing new is formed to pay for it — while **combustions and
combinations are exothermic**. Among any list of furnace reactions, the carbonate
decomposition is the one absorbing heat.
∴ CaCO₃ ⟶ CaO + CO₂.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|1||0|0:
Work in **moles** and remember that oxalic acid is **dibasic**.
**Step 1 — moles of NaOH.** Its molar mass is 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹:
n(NaOH) = 0·064 / 40 = **1·6 × 10⁻³ mol**
**Step 2 — moles of oxalic acid.** Oxalic acid, H₂C₂O₄, has **two** replaceable hydrogens, so
one mole of it neutralises **two** moles of NaOH:
H₂C₂O₄ + 2NaOH ⟶ Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O
n(acid) = 1·6 × 10⁻³ / 2 = **0·8 × 10⁻³ mol**
**Step 3 — convert the volume.**
25 cm³ = **0·025 L**
**Step 4 — molarity.**
M = 0·8 × 10⁻³ / 0·025 = **0·032 mol L⁻¹** ✓
The **basicity of 2** is the step the question turns on. Treating the neutralisation as 1 : 1
gives 1·6 × 10⁻³/0·025 = 0·064 M — which is option (3), and is simply the mass of NaOH
reappearing as a concentration, a coincidence the examiner has exploited.
A useful cross-check in **normality**: the acid is 0·032 M × 2 = 0·064 N, and
0·064 N × 25 cm³ = 1·6 milliequivalents, which matches 0·064 g ÷ 40 = 1·6 mmol of the
monoacidic base ✓
∴ 0·032.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|2||0|0:
Take the four statements in turn.
**(1) Energies of stationary states in hydrogen-like atoms are inversely proportional to the
square of the principal quantum number** ✓ **correct.** Eₙ = −13·6 Z²/n² eV, so the magnitude
falls as 1/n²: −13·6, −3·4, −1·51, −0·85 eV for n = 1 to 4.
**(2) The radius of the first orbit of He⁺ is half that of hydrogen** ✓ **correct.**
rₙ = 52·9 n²/Z pm, and helium has Z = 2, so r₁(He⁺) = 52·9/2 = 26·45 pm, exactly half of
hydrogen's 52·9 pm.
**(3) The angular (azimuthal) quantum number signifies the shape of the orbital** ✓
**correct.** l = 0 gives a spherical s orbital, l = 1 a dumb-bell p, l = 2 a cloverleaf d.
**(4) The total number of nodes for a 3s orbital is three** ✗ **not correct** — this is the
answer.
The formula is
**total nodes = n − 1**
so for 3s, n = 3 and the total is **2**, not 3.
Breaking them down: **angular nodes = l = 0** (an s orbital is spherical, with no nodal
plane), and **radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 3 − 0 − 1 = 2**. So the 3s orbital has two spherical
shells of zero electron density and nothing else — two nodes in all.
The three counts are worth keeping together: angular = l, radial = n − l − 1, total = n − 1.
∴ statement (4).
kcet|Chemistry|2014|5||0|0:
For an ideal gas the density is
d = PM / RT
so with the same gas (M fixed), **d ∝ P/T**. The maximum density is simply the largest value
of **P/T**.
Work out the ratio for each, with P in atm and T in kelvin:
**(1) 0·5 atm, 273 K** ⟶ 0·5/273 = **0·00183**
**(2) 4 atm, 500 K** ⟶ 4/500 = **0·0080** ✓ largest
**(3) 2 atm, 600 K** ⟶ 2/600 = **0·00333**
**(4) 6 atm, 1092 K** ⟶ 6/1092 = **0·00549**
So the density is greatest at **4 atm and 500 K** ✓ — option (2).
The two influences pull in opposite directions and must be weighed together: **raising the
pressure** packs the molecules closer and increases the density, while **raising the
temperature** expands the gas and decreases it. Option (4) has the highest pressure of all,
six atmospheres, but its temperature is more than twice that of option (2), and the
temperature wins.
That is why the comparison cannot be made by looking at P or T alone — only the **ratio**
settles it, and computing four small quotients is the whole of the work.
The identity of the gas is irrelevant to the comparison, since M cancels; carbon monoxide is
named only to fix that it is the same gas throughout.
∴ 4 atm and 500 K.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|6||0|0:
The hydrogens of an **active methylene group** are acidic because the carbanion left behind
is stabilised by **delocalisation into the groups on either side**. The more effectively
those groups withdraw electrons, the more acidic the CH₂.
A **ketone** carbonyl is a better electron sink than an **ester** carbonyl. The reason is
that in an ester the carbonyl is already partly satisfied by the lone pair of its –OR oxygen,
which donates into the C=O by resonance; a ketone has no such internal donor, so it takes
more charge from the carbanion.
Now rank the three:
**(b) CH₃CO–CH₂–COCH₃** — acetylacetone, flanked by **two ketones**. Best stabilisation,
**most acidic**, pKa ≈ **9**
**(a) CH₃CO–CH₂–COOC₂H₅** — ethyl acetoacetate, flanked by **one ketone and one ester**.
Intermediate, pKa ≈ **11**
**(c) C₂H₅OOC–CH₂–COOC₂H₅** — diethyl malonate, flanked by **two esters**. Weakest, pKa ≈ **13**
So acid strength decreases as **b > a > c** ✓ — option (4).
The figures show how striking the effect is: acetylacetone at pKa 9 is about as acidic as
phenol, and a million times more acidic than an ordinary ketone such as acetone (pKa 20).
That acidity is what makes these compounds useful — a mild base generates the carbanion, and
the **acetoacetic ester** and **malonic ester** syntheses are both built on it.
∴ b > a > c.
kcet|Chemistry|2014|9||0|0:
Gold sol is the classic **lyophobic** colloid, prepared by reducing a dilute gold salt. Take
the four descriptions.
**(1) A lyophobic colloid** ✓ **true.** There is no affinity between the gold particles and
water; the sol is only kinetically stable and is irreversibly coagulated by a trace of
electrolyte.
**(2) Negatively charged colloid** ✓ **true.** The particles adsorb negative ions from the
solution, and the resulting like charges repel one another — which is the only thing keeping
the sol from coagulating. In electrophoresis the particles migrate to the **anode**.
**(4) A multimolecular colloid** ✓ **true.** Each colloidal particle is an **aggregate of
thousands of gold atoms** held by van der Waals forces, with an overall diameter in the
1–1000 nm range. That is exactly what 'multimolecular' means.
**(3) A macromolecular colloid** ✗ **not true** — this is the answer.
A **macromolecular** colloid is one in which each particle is a **single very large
molecule** — starch, cellulose, protein, or a synthetic polymer. Gold has no such molecules:
it is an element whose atoms clump together into particles. The particle is an **aggregate**,
not a molecule.
The distinction is the standard three-way classification of colloids: **multimolecular**
(aggregates of small particles, like gold or sulphur sols), **macromolecular** (single large
molecules, like starch) and **associated** (micelles, like soap above its critical
concentration).
∴ a macro molecular colloid.
